Stage 1 Diagnostics

Convergence, tuning, coefficient plausibility, conditional-forecast sanity, and fit – for all 11 country satellite models

1. Convergence

R/diagnostics.R provides diagnostics_grid() / save_stage1_plots(), wrapping koma’s trace_plot(), running_mean_plot(), and acf_plot() across every stochastic equation in every country. The full set – 3 plot kinds x 6-7 equations x 11 countries – is saved under reports/stage1/<iso2>/. Below is one representative country (Germany); the remaining ten follow an identical pattern and are linked at the end of this section.

Automated stability flag. check_running_mean_stability() recovers each coefficient’s raw per-draw values from koma’s cumulative running_mean(), restricts to the last third of the (post-grace) chain, and flags a coefficient if that tail’s drift (second half’s mean minus first half’s) exceeds 2 Monte Carlo standard errors. Applied to every coefficient in every equation in every country:

Running-mean stability: 0/291 coefficients flagged across all 11 countries.
country n_flagged n_coefficients
at 0 26
be 0 26
de 0 26
es 0 26
fr 0 26
gr 0 26
ie 0 26
it 0 26
nl 0 26
pt 0 26
us 0 31

Zero coefficients, in any country, show an undecayed drift in the last third of the chain. Combined with the trace/ACF plots (visually well-mixed, no wandering or stuck chains – see the linked plots below), stage 1’s MCMC chains are judged converged everywhere.

Full plot sets: reports/stage1/at/, .../be/, .../de/, .../es/, .../fr/, .../gr/, .../ie/, .../it/, .../nl/, .../pt/, .../us/.

2. Acceptance rates and tau tuning

koma’s own target band is 20-60% (koma:::get_default_acceptance_prob(); see CLAUDE.md for why the code, not the vignette prose, is authoritative). At the baseline tau = 1.1 every equation carries by default, several countries had one or two equations just over the 60% ceiling:

Equations outside the 20-60% band at baseline tau = 1.1.
country equation acceptance_rate flagged
at at_consumption 0.6095 TRUE
at at_investment 0.6135 TRUE
be be_consumption 0.6215 TRUE
de de_imports 0.6040 TRUE
de de_long_rate 0.6045 TRUE
gr gr_long_rate 0.6065 TRUE
es es_investment 0.6040 TRUE
fr fr_consumption 0.6040 TRUE
fr fr_imports 0.6005 TRUE
it it_investment 0.6035 TRUE
nl nl_consumption 0.6035 TRUE
us us_imports 0.6120 TRUE

tune_tau() (R/diagnostics.R) re-estimates the country with every currently-flagged equation’s tau doubled (koma’s own documented “doubling tau halves the acceptance rate” rule of thumb), leaving in-band equations untouched, and repeats until every equation is in-band or max_iter is hit. This is a full re-estimate each round – a tau setting is not part of koma’s symbolic warm-start comparison, so nothing short of a full re-estimate would apply it. Run with max_iter = 3:

Before/after: every country converges to an in-band acceptance rate within 1-2 re-estimation rounds.
country iterations converged n_flagged_final tuned_equations
at 1 TRUE 0 at_consumption, at_investment
be 2 TRUE 0 be_consumption, be_imports
de 1 TRUE 0 de_imports, de_long_rate
gr 2 TRUE 0 gr_long_rate, gr_investment
es 2 TRUE 0 es_investment, es_consumption
fr 1 TRUE 0 fr_consumption, fr_imports
ie 0 TRUE 0 (none needed)
it 2 TRUE 0 it_investment, it_consumption
nl 1 TRUE 0 nl_consumption
pt 0 TRUE 0 (none needed)
us 1 TRUE 0 us_imports

All 11 countries converge (every equation in-band) within at most 2 rounds; Ireland and Portugal needed no adjustment at all. tau never had to move past 2.2 (one doubling from 1.1) except where two rounds were needed. This is a mild band violation, not a modelling problem: acceptance rates were 60.0-62.2%, a couple of points over the ceiling, not the kind of pathological (near-0% or near-100%) rate that would indicate a badly scaled proposal.

3. Coefficient plausibility

Three sign checks, applied to each country’s coefficient_table() posterior means (90% credible intervals from ci_low/ci_high) via sign_checks():

  • mpc_in_0_1: consumption’s loading on GDP should be a plausible marginal propensity to consume, in (0, 1).
  • import_elasticity_positive: imports’ loading on domestic demand should be positive.
  • long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate: the long-rate equation’s loading on the policy rate (euro-area or US) should be positive.

6 of 33 checks fail, in 6 of 11 countries (GR, ES, IE, IT, PT, US). The failures cluster in one place: long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate fails in GR, IT, PT, and US, each with an estimate near zero or slightly negative (-0.13 to -0.001) rather than a clear positive loading – the long-rate equation’s short estimation sample and lag structure leaves this coefficient weakly identified in several countries, not systematically wrong-signed by a large margin. Separately, ES’s marginal propensity to consume is 1.20 (above 1, an implausibly high sensitivity of consumption to GDP) and IE’s is effectively zero (-0.003) – consistent with Ireland’s well-documented national-accounts distortions from multinational activity (see data_eamdqd.R’s note on the 2015 GDP break) showing up again here. import_elasticity_positive never fails: every country’s imports load positively on domestic demand, as expected.

4. Conditional-forecast sanity

conditional_forecast_check() imposes two scenarios on each country’s existing stage-1 fit (options = list(approximate = TRUE), a deterministic point forecast from posterior-mean coefficients, since koma::forecast() is otherwise stochastic between repeated calls on the same fit – see the function’s roxygen for the verified magnitudes):

  • oil: oil price level +50% from the forecast start – expect <iso2>_prices to rise.
  • policy: policy rate +100bp from the forecast start – expect <iso2>_gdp to fall.
Conditional-forecast sign check, by country and scenario (diff = scenario - baseline).

at policy at_gdp 0.0000 0.0000 negative FALSE

us policy us_gdp 6.3731 0.6937 negative FALSE

Oil scenario: passes in all 11 countries. A +50% oil-price level shock raises <iso2>_prices at every horizon, in every country, as expected – the largest effect is on impact (horizon 1) and decays through the horizon, consistent with the shock being a one-time level step feeding a diff_log-scale equation.

Policy scenario: fails in all 11 countries, but not for the same reason in all of them. In the stage-1 template (stage1_spec()), <iso2>_long_rate is the only equation the policy rate feeds into, and nothing downstream of long_rate exists at stage 1 – so for the ten euro-area countries, where ea_policy_rate is exogenous and the shock is imposed by rewriting its exogenous path (shock_exogenous_level()), GDP simply cannot move: the diff is exactly 0.0000 at every horizon. That is a structural property of the stage-1 specification (each country’s own small system, isolated from the rest), not a sign error to fix here; building the transmission channel (long rate -> investment/consumption, or a direct GDP channel) is exactly the kind of cross-equation interaction stage 2’s joint system is for.

The US is different, and worse: us_policy_rate is endogenous (its own Taylor-rule equation), so the shock is imposed via koma::forecast(restrictions = ) instead of rewriting an exogenous series. That does move us_gdp – but in the wrong direction: +6.37 at horizon 1, decaying to +0.69 by horizon 4, i.e. GDP rises after a 100bp hike. There is still no structural channel from us_policy_rate to us_gdp in the stage-1 template, so this is not a real transmission effect; conditioning one endogenous variable’s path in forecast(restrictions = ) perturbs the other equations’ draws through their residual correlation (the Gibbs sampler’s joint error structure), not through any regressor. That residual correlation is apparently positive here, producing a spurious, wrong-signed reaction rather than the euro-area countries’ clean “no effect”. This is worth flagging explicitly for stage 2: once us_policy_rate (or ea_policy_rate) has a real structural GDP channel, this artefact should disappear on its own; until then, nothing in this scenario’s US result should be read as GDP being genuinely more policy-sensitive one way or the other.

Both patterns are retained deliberately as a regression check across stages: the euro-area “no effect” and the US “wrong-signed residual leakage” should both resolve once stage 2 adds a genuine long-rate -> demand channel.

Most equations sit in a tight 0.2-2.6 percentage-point RMSE band. Two outliers stand out: IE investment (23.1pp) and NL investment (11.0pp) are far higher than every other equation, in any country. Ireland’s investment series is known to be distorted by multinational capital-relocation swings (again, the same national-accounts issue flagged in data_eamdqd.R and surfacing again in section 3’s MPC check); the Dutch figure, while smaller, points at the same kind of volatile, poorly-explained investment series rather than a specification error shared with the rest of the model.

Pseudo-out-of-sample RMSE (2016Q1-2019Q4, expanding window)

pseudo_oos_rmse() wraps koma’s model_evaluation(): re-estimating with the sample expanded by one quarter at a time, forecasting horizon = 4 quarters ahead, and reporting RMSE on levels (koma’s own default) – not comparable in magnitude to the in-sample table above (see that function’s roxygen for why evaluate_on_levels = FALSE was tried and rejected). RMSE rises with horizon in every country, as expected of a compounding expanding-window forecast. The rate-scale equations (prices, long_rate) stay in a modest low-single-digit range even at 4 quarters out. The level-scale equations’ RMSEs look large in absolute terms, but that is a unit artefact of levels in national-accounts index/currency terms, not evidence of poor fit by itself – read them relative to each series’ own level (e.g. against panel$<iso2>_investment), not against the in-sample table’s percent-growth RMSEs.

6. Per-country verdicts

Each paragraph below is generated from the tables in sections 1-5; the underlying data (not prose) is what to trust if a future re-run changes the numbers.

AT (Austria). Clean convergence, no stability flags. One equation (at_investment, alongside at_consumption) needed one round of tau tuning to reach the acceptance band; both converged easily. All three sign checks pass. Oil scenario correct; policy scenario shows the expected (stage-1-only) absence of a GDP channel. In-sample and pseudo-OOS RMSEs are unremarkable. Usable as a stage-2 building block with no reservations.

BE (Belgium). Clean convergence. Acceptance tuning took two rounds (be_consumption, then be_imports) but fully converged. All sign checks pass. Oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block with no reservations.

DE (Germany). Clean convergence, one round of tuning (de_imports, de_long_rate). All sign checks pass, including the long-rate/policy-rate loading – Germany is the one large country where that coefficient is unambiguously well-signed. RMSEs in line with the cross-country norm. Usable as a stage-2 building block with no reservations; if any single country’s stage-1 fit should anchor cross-checks on stage 2, this is it.

GR (Greece). Clean convergence, two rounds of tuning (gr_long_rate, gr_investment), both converged. The long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate check fails (-0.13): plausible given Greece’s 2015 capital-controls episode and the one interpolated observation at gr_long_rate 2015Q3 (see CLAUDE.md) – the long-rate equation is estimated through a genuinely disrupted bond market. Other checks pass; oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block, but treat gr_long_rate as the weakest equation in this country’s system and do not lean on its policy-rate sensitivity for anything downstream.

ES (Spain). Clean convergence, two rounds of tuning (es_investment, es_consumption), converged. The mpc_in_0_1 check fails: consumption’s loading on GDP is 1.20, above the plausible range, implying consumption over-reacts to GDP growth one-for-one plus some. Import elasticity and long-rate checks pass; oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block, but the consumption equation’s GDP sensitivity should be revisited (priors, sample window, or an added regressor) before its multiplier effects are trusted quantitatively.

FR (France). Clean convergence, one round of tuning (fr_consumption, fr_imports). All sign checks pass. Oil scenario correct; RMSEs unremarkable. Usable as a stage-2 building block with no reservations.

IE (Ireland). Clean convergence – and, notably, no tau tuning was even needed: every equation was already in-band at baseline. But this is the model with the most serious plausibility issues elsewhere: the mpc_in_0_1 check fails (estimate effectively zero, -0.003, not a plausible consumption-GDP link), and ie_investment’s in-sample RMSE (23.1pp) is by far the largest of any equation in any country. Both point at the same well-documented cause – Ireland’s national accounts are distorted by multinational capital and IP relocation (the same issue behind the 2015 GDP break flagged in data_eamdqd.R). Oil scenario still correct (that channel is unaffected). Usable as a stage-2 building block only with caution: the consumption and investment equations are not reliable in their current form, and Ireland’s results should be flagged as low-confidence in any stage-2/stage-3 output that depends on them.

IT (Italy). Clean convergence, two rounds of tuning (it_investment, it_consumption), converged. long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate fails, though only marginally (-0.001, essentially zero rather than meaningfully negative) – a weak-identification result, not a strong-sign violation. Other checks pass; oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block; the long-rate equation’s policy sensitivity is negligible rather than wrong-signed and is a reasonable candidate to firm up once stage 2 shares information across countries.

NL (Netherlands). Clean convergence, one round of tuning (nl_consumption). All sign checks pass. The one blemish is nl_investment’s in-sample RMSE (11.0pp), the second-largest of any equation after Ireland’s – smaller and less structurally explained, but still the country’s weakest equation. Oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block; keep an eye on the investment equation’s fit, but nothing here blocks using the model as specified.

PT (Portugal). Clean convergence, and like Ireland, no tau tuning was needed. The long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate check fails (-0.09). Import elasticity and MPC pass; oil scenario correct. Usable as a stage-2 building block; treat the long-rate equation the same way as Greece’s and Italy’s – weak, not wrong.

US (United States). Clean convergence, one round of tuning (us_imports). The long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate check fails (-0.02, essentially zero) – notably, this is the one country where the policy rate is endogenous (its own Taylor-rule equation, us_policy_rate), yet the long-rate loading is still not positive, suggesting the weak identification seen in GR/IT/PT is a template-wide long-rate specification issue rather than something specific to the euro-area policy-rate sharing arrangement. us_policy_rate’s own acceptance rate (39.2%) and us_long_rate’s (40.4%) sit comfortably mid-band, well clear of any tuning need. Oil scenario correct. The policy scenario is the one genuinely concerning result in this report: because us_policy_rate is endogenous, the +100bp shock is imposed via forecast(restrictions = ), and us_gdp moves the wrong way (up, not down) – a spurious effect leaking in through the Gibbs sampler’s residual correlation across equations rather than any real regressor link (see section 4). Usable as a stage-2 building block for its own equations, but do not use this country’s conditional-forecast machinery for anything policy-rate-related until stage 2 gives us_policy_rate a genuine GDP channel; until then, treat any US policy-scenario output as an artefact, not a result.

Cross-country pattern

The long_rate_loads_on_policy_rate check is the recurring failure (GR, IT, PT, US – four of six total sign-check failures), and it fails in both euro-area and US variants of the identical equation template. That points at the equation itself (<iso2>_long_rate ~ <iso2>_prices + policy_rate + <iso2>_long_rate.L(1)) being under-specified for a positive policy-rate loading generally, not a country-specific data problem – worth revisiting the template (an additional lag, a term capturing sovereign risk/spread dynamics) before stage 2, since every country’s long-rate equation inherits the same structure.

Every country converges cleanly (acceptance and stability) and every country’s oil-price transmission is correctly signed. The policy-rate-to- GDP scenario failing everywhere is expected and not a defect – it is the gap stage 2 exists to close. With that caveat, all 11 stage-1 country models are usable as stage-2 building blocks; ES and IE need the most attention (consumption equation) before their multiplier implications should be trusted, and GR/IT/PT/US share a long-rate equation that is weak but not wrong-signed in a way that would corrupt a joint estimation.

Eight-quarter forecast

8 quarters from 2023Q1 to 2024Q4, 1000 posterior draws. The whole window is already observed, so this is an out-of-sample check rather than a projection.

Every fan below is the filtered predictive interval: koma constrains no draw to be stationary, so a draw whose quarterly growth exceeds 100% in absolute value is dropped before the quantiles are taken, exactly as score_forecast() does when it scores a backtest. The solid band is the 25th-75th percentile of what survives, the faint band the 10th-90th, the dark line their median, and the grey line the realised path where one exists. Across the variables shown, 0.4% of draws are discarded as explosive at horizon 1, rising to 2.8% at horizon 8 (worst: gr_gdp at 21.0%). A variable whose discarded share climbs steeply is one whose fan understates the model’s true uncertainty, so read the tail of a wide fan as an ordering rather than a number.

The panels are clipped, and that is worth saying plainly. Eight quarters out, the 10-90 interval on quarterly growth spans tens of percentage points in every stage of this project – an honest number, and one that makes the median invisible if the axis is scaled to contain it. Each panel is therefore scaled to its inner band, and the outer band runs to the panel edge rather than being drawn in full. Nothing is concealed: the table at the end of this section reports the untruncated bounds.

The level paths are anchored on conditionally-filled values, not observed ones. koma takes the anchor from the end of the fit’s own ts_data, and this stage fills 2022Q4 before forecasting. The worst discrepancy is ie_investment, anchored at 5.918e+04 against an observed 2.311e+04 – 156.1% out – and the median across all variables is 4.2%. A level gap at horizon 1 is therefore inherited from the fill, not produced by the forecast. Read the rate chart, which is unaffected.

A forecast this long needs the exogenous series to reach the end of the horizon, and they do not: every one of them stops at the fit’s own native forecast end. extend_forecast_horizon() carries each one forward on its trailing four-quarter average growth – a momentum continuation, not a view on oil markets or world trade – and koma would otherwise have silently returned a shorter horizon than the one requested.
